title: Exile
hook: since 1959 the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived in exile; a sorrow held with care

segments.voice: Yesterday: four schools, and your line, four streams. Did you notice what people shared before you noticed their differences? Day three hundred sixteen.

If you had one night to leave your home, and you could never come back, what would you carry? Not what you'd pack. What you'd carry: the songs, the recipes, the prayers your grandmother said, the way your family does things. In March 1959, tens of thousands of Tibetans faced some version of that question. Many of the practices you've met in these two weeks, the chants, the mandalas, the teachers, reached the rest of the world because people carried them over the mountains. Today: exile.
screen: `ONE NIGHT TO LEAVE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `OVER THE MOUNTAINS, 1959.`

segments.voice: Here is the history, told plainly. Chinese forces entered Tibet in 1950. In March 1959, after an uprising in Lhasa, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, then twenty-three years old, left the city at night. He crossed the Himalayas for about two weeks, on horseback and on foot, and reached India. Tens of thousands of Tibetans followed him, and more came in later years. India gave land and shelter. The hill town of Dharamsala became the Dalai Lama's home and the seat of the Tibetan administration in exile. People hold strong and very different views about Tibet's politics, and the Chinese government describes these events very differently. This lesson stays with the people and the practice. And here is what the people carried. Monks who had memorized whole texts recited them so they could be written down again. The great monasteries of Sera, Drepung and Ganden were founded anew in the fields of south India, and the debating courtyards filled with clapping and questions once more. Settlements grew in India and Nepal, and later in Europe and North America. Teachers who would never have left Tibet began teaching in cities all over the world. Tibetans often speak of this with deep grief, and also with a steadiness that visitors notice. The Dalai Lama has often said that those who drove them out are also to be held with compassion. That's the sorrow held with care: not pretending it didn't happen, not letting it turn into hatred. A tradition, carried on foot, into exile.
screen: `MARCH 1959 — A NIGHT CROSSING.` · `DHARAMSALA, AND FIELDS IN THE SOUTH.` · `MEMORIZED TEXTS, WRITTEN AGAIN.` · `GRIEF, WITHOUT HATRED.` · then, large: `CARRIED INTO EXILE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, hold them in metta. Picture Tibetans living far from the land their families came from: an old monk in south India, a teenager in a city apartment who has never seen Tibet. Silently offer them the metta phrases you learned, may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease. If you'd like, widen it to everyone, anywhere, who has had to leave home. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Since 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived outside Tibet, carrying their practice with them: a sorrow held with care.
Your line: carried into exile. Today, name one thing from your own family or past that you'd carry anywhere, and thank whoever carried it to you. Day three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Tibetan communities in exile, centered on Dharamsala and settlements in India and Nepal, have re-founded major monasteries, schools and institutes, and many Tibetans mark March 10, the anniversary of the 1959 uprising, with prayers and gatherings.

fork.setup: you're a monk who has fled with nothing but your robes. your monastery's library is gone. what do you do?
options: give up on the old teachings.
recite the texts you memorized so they can be written down again.
wait until you can go back.
fork.reveal: monks who had memorized whole texts recited them, and the teachings were written again, and the monasteries rebuilt, in exile.

original.note: Pali mettā: loving-kindness, the first word of this path, offered today to those living in exile.

trapdoor: what you thought: exile is only a political story.
what it means: a people who carried a whole tradition over the mountains, and hold their grief with care.
what a scholar hears: the exile's re-founded monasteries in Karnataka and its printing of texts helped preserve and spread Tibetan Buddhism worldwide after 1959.

notes: Politically sensitive: the script states dates (1950, March 1959), notes that the Chinese government describes events differently, and stays with the people and the practice. Keeper and owner should review tone.
Journey length (about two weeks) and the Dalai Lama's age (23): confirm.
'Tens of thousands followed' (often given as about 80,000 in the first years): confirm.
Sera, Drepung and Ganden re-founded in Karnataka (Bylakuppe and Mundgod): confirm.
The statement about compassion for those who drove Tibetans out paraphrases many public talks by the Dalai Lama.
Metta phrases in the practice are the path's own practice phrases from Camp 3, not a new prayer.
